title: Draw your skill tree: map what you can do, choose your next branch
description: Video games show a character's abilities as a branching tree. Draw your own — real skills you have, connected to the ones they unlock — and your next step stops being a guess.
author: SparkKindly · AI-assisted

body.heading: Draw the trunk and the branches you have
paragraphs: Take a large sheet of paper. Near the bottom, draw a trunk and label it with a broad area of your life: cooking, music, work, making things. Now add branches for skills you genuinely have, however modest: “can season a soup”, “can play three songs”, “can fix a puncture”.
Be honest and be generous at once: modest skills count, because branches are built from them. Most people are startled by how much tree they already have.

body.heading: Add the branches you could grow
paragraphs: From each existing branch, sketch thinner, dashed branches for the skills it nearly unlocks. Three songs nearly unlock a fourth, and then playing with others. Seasoning a soup nearly unlocks stocks, and then sauces.
Look for the dashed branch that appears in several places, or the one you keep glancing back at. That is information about what you actually want, delivered without a single personality quiz.

body.heading: Choose one branch for this season
paragraphs: Circle exactly one dashed branch and write beside it the smallest first step: one lesson, one recipe, one phone call. Stick the tree where you will see it, and add to it in a different colour as skills land.
A year of seasons, one branch at a time, turns a drawing into a record of growth you can literally see — and a standing answer to the question “what should I learn next?”

takeaway: Map the skills you have as branches, sketch the ones they unlock, and choose one branch per season to grow.
materials: Pens or pencils in two colours
A wall or door to display the finished tree
supervision: Independent activity for adults and older teens; younger children can draw a tree with an adult's help.
safetyNotes: Use paper and pens safely; no personal information needs to leave the house — the tree is for your wall, not for posting with identifying details.
